title: A Comparative Study of Self-Retrieval Augmented Generation and Traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
body_md:
## Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with language generation to improve the factual grounding of responses produced by large language models. However, traditional RAG systems may generate unsupported claims when retrieved information is incomplete, irrelevant, or insufficient to answer a user's query. Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) addresses this limitation by incorporating mechanisms for assessing retrieved evidence, determining the need for additional retrieval, and evaluating generated responses. This paper presents a comparative study of traditional RAG and Self-RAG for evidence-grounded question answering. The study examines their retrieval strategies, response generation processes, evidence assessment capabilities, and approaches to reducing unsupported information. The proposed evaluation framework considers retrieval relevance, answer faithfulness, response completeness, and the ability to identify insufficient evidence. The analysis aims to provide insights into the advantages and limitations of adaptive retrieval and self-reflection in knowledge-intensive question-answering systems. The findings can support the development of more reliable document-based question-answering applications.

## Introduction

. Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as an approach for improving the responses of large language models by providing relevant information from external knowledge sources. Traditional RAG systems retrieve documents based on a user query and pass the retrieved context to a language model for response generation. Although this approach can improve access to domain-specific information, its effectiveness depends on the relevance and completeness of the retrieved documents.

Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) extends this process by incorporating reflection mechanisms that help assess retrieval requirements, evidence, and generated responses. These capabilities may support more adaptive and evidence-grounded question answering.

This study investigates the differences between traditional RAG and Self-RAG in document-based question answering. It focuses on retrieval behavior, evidence evaluation, response faithfulness, and the handling of queries for which supporting information is unavailable.

## Related Work

II. Related Work

This section should review existing research on retrieval-augmented generation, adaptive retrieval, and self-reflective language model systems.

Organize the discussion into:

Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Self-RAG and reflection-based generation.

Retrieval evaluation and response faithfulness.

Hallucination mitigation in language models.

## Methodology

III. Methodology

The study compares a traditional RAG pipeline with a Self-RAG-inspired pipeline for evidence-grounded question answering. Both approaches use a document collection, a retrieval component, and a language model for response generation.

Traditional RAG workflow:

Query → Document Retrieval → Context Construction → Response Generation

Self-RAG-inspired workflow:

Query → Document Retrieval → Evidence Assessment → Response Generation → Claim Verification → Self-Correction (when required)

The evaluation should use the same document collection, query set, and relevant model conditions where feasible. Metrics may include retrieval relevance, answer faithfulness, completeness, response latency, and unsupported claim rate.

Clearly document the embedding model, vector database, language model, chunking strategy, retrieval configuration, and evaluation dataset.

## Results

IV. Results

This section must contain the results of your actual experiments.

Suggested subsections:

A. Retrieval Performance: Compare the relevance and coverage of retrieved evidence.

B. Answer Faithfulness: Analyze whether generated claims are supported by retrieved sources.

C. Missing Evidence Handling: Evaluate how the systems respond when relevant information is unavailable.

D. Response Efficiency: Compare latency, token usage, and computational overhead.

## Discussion

V. Discussion

Discuss the observed differences between the evaluated systems and connect the results to your research objectives.

Consider whether reflection mechanisms improve evidence assessment, whether additional verification introduces latency, and how the systems behave when the knowledge base does not contain sufficient information.

## Limitations

VI. Limitations

The study may be affected by the choice of datasets, retrieval configuration, language model, and evaluation criteria. Differences in model capabilities or system configurations can influence the comparison.

Additional limitations may include the size of the evaluation dataset, the cost of repeated generation and verification, the difficulty of measuring faithfulness automatically, and the generalizability of findings to other domains.

## Conclusion

VII. Conclusion

This paper presents a comparative study of traditional RAG and Self-RAG for evidence-grounded question answering. The study examines their retrieval and generation workflows, evidence assessment strategies, and approaches to handling unsupported information.

The experimental findings should be used to explain the observed strengths and limitations of each approach. Future work may investigate improved retrieval strategies, efficient reflection mechanisms, multimodal evidence, and evaluation methods for reliable question answering.

Update the final conclusion after completing the experiments so that it reflects the actual results of the study.

[2] A. Asai, Z. Wu, Y. Wang, A. Sil, and H. Hajishirzi, "Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection," in *The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)*, 2024.

[3] S. Gao, Y. Fang, Y. Liu, Z. Zhao, K. Xu, T. J. Cui, and others, "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey," arXiv preprint arXiv:2312.10997, 2023.

[4] S. Min, M. Lewis, H. Hajishirzi, and L. Zettlemoyer, "Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?" in *Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing*, 2022.

[5] O. A. G. A. et al., "FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation," in *Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing*, 2023.

[6] S. Yao, D. Yu, J. Zhao, I. Shafran, T. L. Griffiths, Y. Cao, and K. Narasimhan, "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models," in *International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)*, 2023.
